items.answer: Nitrogen deficiency: older leaves turn pale yellow (chlorosis) starting from leaf tips, stunted growth, reduced tillering, poor grain filling. Management: apply urea or ammonium sulfate in split doses (basal + top-dress at tillering and panicle initiation). Iron toxicity: bronzing/brown spots on older leaves, root damage from excess Fe2+ in waterlogged acidic soils. Key difference: N deficiency is uniform yellowing; iron toxicity shows distinct brown/bronze patches. Iron toxicity needs drainage and liming; N deficiency needs fertilization.

prompt.content: Describe the signs and management of nitrogen deficiency in rice paddies. How does it differ from iron toxicity symptoms?

items.answer: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to root zones (90-95% efficiency), higher upfront cost but lower long-term water cost, 20-50% yield increase, best for row crops, orchards, and water-scarce regions. Flood irrigation is 40-60% efficient, low setup cost but high water waste, suitable for rice paddies and flat terrain with abundant water. Choose drip for high-value crops and arid regions; flood for rice or when water is abundant and labor is cheap.

prompt.content: What are the key differences between drip irrigation and flood irrigation in terms of water efficiency, cost, and crop yield? When should a farmer choose one over the other?
